title: The Evening Brief: Control tested as scandals, injuries, and returns reshape fall sports
dek: Tuesday evening finds programs across football, baseball, and tennis confronting the gap between what they claim and what events are forcing them to prove. Belichick denies loss of control as an investigation deepens. Judge returns to the Yankees. The SEC votes Thursday on expelling LSU. And multiple programs absorb opening-week injuries while their true depth remains unknown.
author: GoCheckMySports
key_fact: Institutional control is no longer a claim but a live question being tested by investigation, injury, legal action, and competitive return across multiple sports simultaneously.
bottom_line: Tuesday evening reveals a day in which institutional claims of control, compliance, and readiness collided with real-time pressure. Belichick denies loss of control while an investigation widens. The SEC votes Thursday on expelling LSU despite legal obstacles. Judge returns to the Yankees after three months out. Notre Dame and Washington absorb opening-week injuries with depth and return timelines still unknown. And Pietersen rejoins England's white-ball program as a mentor after 12 years in exile, a return that Root endorses but the organization has never formally reconciled. The coming days will test whether these claims hold: the investigation continues with no announced conclusion, the SEC vote occurs Thursday, Judge plays Colorado tonight, Notre Dame faces Rice on Saturday, and Pietersen joins the Sri Lanka series next week.
body: The day's through-line is institutional control under pressure. Bill Belichick said Monday his UNC football program maintains an atmosphere of compliance, but the university's investigation continues to widen. General manager Michael Lombardi resigned on September 3 after being placed on leave, and investigators have expanded their scope to include questions about alleged drug use and inappropriate relationships among assistant coaches and recruiting staff. Belichick, whose contract mandates he promote an atmosphere of compliance, declined to discuss specifics and said he understands the investigative team's work. When asked if he saw such an atmosphere daily, he said, "If you're around here every day, I think you'd see it." That answer carries no timeline: the investigation remains open and no conclusion has been announced.

The same pressure appeared elsewhere in college football. The SEC scheduled a vote for Thursday on expelling LSU, filing an amended federal complaint Tuesday that seeks to declare the conference has the power to do so. The dispute centers on LSU's recruitment of former NFL players. SEC bylaws require a two-thirds majority of conference presidents to expel a member, but a Louisiana state court's prior injunction against SEC enforcement of penalties creates legal uncertainty about whether the conference can carry out any expulsion even if the vote passes. The outcome remains unresolved.

Injury and depth tested multiple programs. Notre Dame defeated Wisconsin 41-13 on September 6 at Lambeau Field but lost two defensive starters to lower left leg injuries in the third quarter. Safety Brauntae Johnson, a junior who recorded four interceptions last season, and defensive tackle Jason Onye, a sixth-year senior who started nine games in 2025, both appeared on the sideline wearing protective boots on their left feet. Coach Marcus Freeman ruled both out for the remainder of the game and said he would meet with medical staff Monday to assess their status for next Saturday's game against Rice. No diagnosis or return timeline has been provided. Washington's running back situation darkened after the Apple Cup win: starting running back Quaid Carr sustained a hand injury requiring surgery, and backup Jayden Limar suffered an elbow injury. Coach Jedd Fisch said both will be out for a while but declined to rule out season-ending status, leaving the Huskies uncertain about who will carry the ball through Big Ten play.

Aaron Judge returned to the Yankees. The reigning AL batting champion was reinstated from the 60-day injured list on September 8 after missing three months due to a right rib stress fracture sustained on April 26. He is expected to play in Tuesday's series opener against Colorado, his first game since May 31. The Yankees were 36-23 when Judge last played and 45-39 without him through Sunday. From June 1 through Sunday, the Yankees ranked 26th in the Majors in runs scored. Manager Aaron Boone said Judge would initially play five to seven innings per game to avoid re-injury.

Elsewhere, Kevin Pietersen joined England's white-ball staff. Joe Root, the only remaining England Test player to have played alongside Pietersen before the latter's controversial 2014 exit, endorsed the appointment as specialist mentor to Brendon McCullum's squad ahead of the 2027 World Cup in South Africa. Pietersen's path back has been lengthy: he was dropped in 2012 after sending messages critical of England players and coaches to members of the South Africa squad, and was barred from recall in 2015 due to a trust issue that remains unresolved in any official statement. Root told the Guardian that Pietersen "was always brilliant" for offering advice, and that he learned a huge amount from him. The Guardian reported the appointment as "a bit of a risk," noting Pietersen "could often be a divisive figure" during his playing career and cautioning that his punditry style may not translate to effective mentorship. Pietersen has also been outspoken in criticism of McCullum's approach to Test cricket. His first mentorship engagement, the Sri Lanka series next week, will be the first test of whether his advisory role avoids the divisions that defined his playing career.

In tennis, Zheng Qinwen advanced to the US Open quarterfinals by defeating Iga Swiatek 7-5, 6-3 on September 7, erasing a 5-0 first-set deficit. The victory marks the second consecutive match in which Zheng has won seven games in a row from 0-5 down, both times against Grand Slam champions. A player winning from that position in consecutive sets against two different opponents is almost unheard of at the highest level; doing so against two Grand Slam title winners has never happened before. Zheng will face second seed Elena Rybakina in the quarterfinals.

In business news, Cricket Australia approved privatization of the Big Bash League, launching a sales process for the Melbourne Renegades with a target date of the 2027-28 season for new ownership. The decision passed despite opposition from New South Wales and Queensland. Rather than proceed with league-wide privatization, Cricket Australia adopted a self-determination model allowing individual states to choose whether and when to sell stakes in their franchises. The Renegades will operate in caretaker mode, managed by Cricket Australia, during the coming 2026-27 season before being sold and rebranded.
